title: The pace of a popular talk
author: @sfiscience
text:
Researchers found that the most popular talks and podcasts moved at slower semantic speeds and had moderate levels of both breadth and circuitousness. (image: Pexels)November 20, 2026Do you dream of going viral? New research by SFI Program Postdoctoral Fellow Shuhao Fu and linguists at Zhejiang University could offer the insights you need. The study, published in Information Processing and Management, assesses the hallmarks of popular TED talks and various podcasts and illuminates why some TED talks succeed while others fail. The key may lie in a mix of the right balance of semantic speed, breadth, and circuitousness.

“People are making all sorts of media content, like talks and short videos,” Fu says. “We’re trying to see if there’s something uniform in there that can predict popularity or guide people to make more popular videos.”

For this new paper, the team combined linguistic theory with Fu’s modeling expertise. They split transcripts of the talks into chunks of about 250 words, preserving whole sentences. Then they used a language-embedding model to encode each chunk’s meaning on a hypersphere, or a sphere with more than three dimensions. By measuring the angular distances between these points, the researchers quantified each talk’s semantic speed, or how quickly it jumped from concept to concept; breadth, or how wide a range of concepts it covered; and circuitousness, or how often it referenced earlier material. They used a similar method for the podcasts.

The researchers found that the most popular talks and podcasts moved at slower semantic speeds and had moderate levels of both breadth and circuitousness. Semantic speed and breadth were linked: talks that covered a narrower range of concepts tended to favor slower speed, while in wider-ranging talks, audiences could handle faster pacing between concepts. Given a talk’s semantic speed, breadth, or circuitousness, they were able to determine an average point where its popularity peaked.

For content creators, these results can “help them make better decisions about how fast they want to progress, how broad a range of concepts they want to cover, and how much they want to circle back to their talk,” Fu says.

The authors are careful to note that these findings aren’t yet generalizable to other contexts. In the future, they hope to apply their method to the transcripts of other forms of media, such as short videos, TV shows, books, and news articles. They’d also like to include other metrics beyond text — for example, by looking at how closely a speaker’s tone of voice matches the material they are discussing.

“We hope to develop a uniform theory or methodology that can be applied to all forms of media,” Fu says.

Sounds like the subject of a future TED talk.
 

Read the paper “Balancing novelty and familiarity: Nonlinear effects of semantic progression on audience engagement” in Information Processing and Management (Oct 12, 2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.ipm.2026.105208
